{"sample_id": "blind-77e1812af50645eaa6f8c162986609e8", "theorem": "Let \( x \) and \( y \) be positive integers. If for each positive integer \( n \) we have that

\[
(n y)^{2}+1 \mid x^{\varphi(n)}-1
\]

prove that \( x=1 \).", "assumptions": [], "domain": "bmo", "explicit_subgoals": [], "candidate_text": "We use Dirichlet’s theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions.

First note the following lemma. If \(\gcd(a,M)=1\), then
\[
\gcd_{\substack{p>2\text{ prime}\\p\equiv a\pmod M}}(p-1)
=\operatorname{lcm}\bigl(2,\gcd(a-1,M)\bigr).
\]
Indeed, the right-hand side divides every \(p-1\). Conversely, fix a prime \(\ell\), and put \(s=v_\ell(M)\) and \(t=v_\ell(a-1)\). If \(t<s\), every integer congruent to \(a\pmod M\) has \(\ell\)-adic valuation \(t\) after subtracting \(1\). If \(t\ge s>0\), the Chinese remainder theorem gives a reduced residue class \(b\) satisfying
\[
b\equiv a\pmod M,\qquad b\equiv1+\ell^s\pmod{\ell^{s+1}}.
\]
Dirichlet’s theorem supplies a prime in this class, for which \(v_\ell(p-1)=s\). If \(s=0\) and \(\ell\) is odd, choose instead a nonzero residue modulo \(\ell\) different from \(1\). For \(\ell=2\) and \(s=0\), choose \(b\equiv3\pmod4\). These choices prove the lemma prime-power by prime-power.

Now fix any positive integer \(n\), and set
\[
M=n^2y^2+1.
\]
We have \(\gcd(n,M)=1\). For every prime \(p\equiv n\pmod M\),
\[
p^2y^2+1\equiv n^2y^2+1\equiv0\pmod M.
\]
The hypothesis applied at the positive integer \(p\) therefore gives
\[
M\mid p^2y^2+1\mid x^{\varphi(p)}-1=x^{p-1}-1.
\]
Thus \(x\) is invertible modulo \(M\). Let \(r\) be its multiplicative order modulo \(M\). Then \(r\mid p-1\) for every prime \(p\equiv n\pmod M\). By the lemma,
\[
r\mid\operatorname{lcm}\bigl(2,\gcd(n-1,M)\bigr).
\]
But
\[
\gcd(n-1,M)=\gcd(n-1,y^2+1),
\]
since \(n\equiv1\pmod{n-1}\). Hence, with the fixed integer
\[
L=\operatorname{lcm}(2,y^2+1),
\]
we have \(r\mid L\). Consequently
\[
n^2y^2+1=M\mid x^L-1
\]
for every positive integer \(n\).

If \(x>1\), then \(x^L-1\) is a fixed positive integer, whereas \(n^2y^2+1\) is unbounded. Choosing \(n\) with \(n^2y^2+1>x^L-1\) contradicts this divisibility. Since \(x\) is positive, it follows that \(x=1\)."}

{"sample_id": "blind-5505136ffca34344b9d8286808d36362", "theorem": "Define $f_{n}:[0,1] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ by the equation $f_{n}(x)=x^{n}$. Show that the sequence $\left(f_{n}\right)$ does not converge uniformly.", "assumptions": [], "domain": "topology", "explicit_subgoals": [], "candidate_text": "For each \(x\in[0,1)\), we have \(x^n\to0\), whereas \(f_n(1)=1\) for every \(n\). Hence the pointwise limit is
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&0\le x<1,\\1,&x=1.\end{cases}
\]
Assume that \((f_n)\) converges uniformly. Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence, so its uniform limit must be \(f\). Set \(\varepsilon=\tfrac14\). For every \(N\in\mathbb Z_+\), choose \(n=N\) and \(x=2^{-1/n}\in[0,1)\). Then \(f(x)=0\), while
\[
|f_n(x)-f(x)|=x^n=\frac12>\varepsilon.
\]
Thus no \(N\) satisfies the uniform-convergence condition. Therefore \((f_n)\) does not converge uniformly on \([0,1]\)."}
